events.description: All systems connecting to DynamoDB in us-east-1 via the public endpoint began experiencing DNS failures; the regional DNS record was empty after the active plan was deleted following an overwrite by a delayed DNS Enactor. Global table replicas in us-east-1 saw prolonged replication lag.
DWFM state checks began to fail because the process depends on DynamoDB; between 11:48 PM and 2:24 AM, leases between DWFM and droplets slowly timed out.
ECS, EKS and Fargate began experiencing container launch failures and cluster scaling delays (until 2:20 AM Oct 20).
Redshift query and cluster operations began failing while DynamoDB endpoints were down (until 2:21 AM Oct 20; some clusters until 4:05 AM Oct 21).
AWS Support Center began failing; it failed over to another region as designed, but an account metadata subsystem returned invalid responses (until 2:40 AM Oct 20).
Lambda began experiencing DynamoDB-related failures preventing function creation and updates and causing invocation errors (until 2:15 PM Oct 20).
AWS Management Console sign-in began failing due to IAM user authentication failures caused by DynamoDB issues (until 1:25 AM Oct 20).
STS began experiencing API errors (until 9:59 AM Oct 20; recovered at 1:19 AM, then errors returned 8:31-9:59 AM).
Amazon Connect began experiencing elevated errors handling calls, chats and cases (until 1:20 AM Oct 20; a second period from 7:04 AM).
Engineers identified DynamoDB's DNS state as the source of the outage.
Temporary mitigations enabled some internal services to connect to DynamoDB and repaired key internal tooling, unblocking further recovery.
Lambda and ECS/EKS/Fargate-related failures ended; ECS, EKS and Fargate recovered at 2:20 AM.
All DNS information for DynamoDB was restored.
EC2 instance launches began failing; DWFM began re-establishing leases, and EC2 APIs returned 'insufficient capacity' errors (until 10:36 AM Oct 20).
Customers could resolve the DynamoDB endpoint and connect as cached DNS records expired.
All global table replicas were fully caught up.
DynamoDB API error rates returned to normal; AWS Support Center impact ended.
Engineers throttled incoming work and began selective restarts of DWFM hosts, clearing queues and allowing leases to be established.
Lambda internal subsystem polling SQS queues, which had failed and not recovered automatically, was restored.

DWFM had established leases with all droplets in us-east-1; new launches began to succeed, though many saw 'request limit exceeded' errors due to throttling. Network Manager began propagating network configurations to newly launched instances, with a backlog.
Network Load Balancer (NLB) began experiencing increased connection errors for some load balancers (until 2:09 PM Oct 20).
Network Manager latencies increased as it worked through the backlog; new instances could launch but lacked network connectivity. Engineers worked to reduce load on Network Manager.
Monitoring detected NLB health check issues caused by new EC2 instances being brought into service before network state propagated; engineers began remediation.

From this time, NLB health check failures triggered Lambda instance terminations, leaving Lambda under-scaled; Lambda throttled asynchronous work. Amazon Connect experienced a second period of errors due to NLB and Lambda impact.
Engineers disabled automatic health check failover for NLB, bringing healthy nodes and targets back into service and resolving connection errors.
Network propagation times returned to normal and new EC2 launches operated normally (connectivity issues for some new instances persisted until 1:50 PM).
Engineers began relaxing EC2 request throttles.
All EC2 APIs and new instance launches operating normally; connectivity issues for newly launched instances resolved.
Automatic DNS health check failover for NLB was re-enabled after EC2 recovered; NLB connection errors ended.
The event ended, per the report overview.
